title: Per-worker mutexes do not synchronize a shared stop signal
applies_when: A Go producer or recursive walker captures a shared error or stop variable that several prefetch workers read while holding different worker mutexes, especially after an early traversal error.
lesson: Trace every read and write of the shared variable, not just whether each worker holds some lock. Different per-worker mutexes do not synchronize the traversal's write. Keep the traversal error owner-local and use a shared atomic or a common synchronization protocol for worker termination. Test normal output, early errors and bounds on the real backend with matched before/after race runs. A deferred stop covers both error and successful early return; stopping future prefetch is not joining an already-running backend call.
avoid_when: A common lock or channel protocol already orders all relevant accesses, or the value is immutable. An atomic flag alone does not unblock stalled I/O or output, join goroutines, or make several related fields a consistent snapshot. Race-detector success covers only exercised schedules. Separate unrelated package-level races from the candidate by running the same command on unchanged source; passing leaf cases cannot override a failing package/process.

evidence.note: Traversal writes captured err while workers read it under distinct listThread locks. Matched native Go race runs reproduce the conflicting accesses; those locks protect worker slots, not the shared traversal error.

Real in-memory nested listing tests cover all/deep/bounded output and initial/child/grandchild errors. Exact fixed source passes five focused race repeats and an object-package race run with disclosed TestDisk2 exclusion and environment skips. Proposed fix uses a walk-owned atomic stop; not full CI, cloud, joined-I/O or performance qualification.
